prompt:
Below are claims about one researcher (TARGET), extracted from their writing, and a sample of claims about four other researchers in the same field (PEERS).

Write 8 statements of how TARGET differs from PEERS on how to design, run and interpret evaluations and alignment experiments. Each starts "Unlike peers, ...". Leave out anything PEERS also hold. At most 250 words in total. Do not name any person, organisation, paper or model. Output only the 8 statements, one per line, each starting "- Unlike peers, ".

TARGET:
- (D1) Prefers evaluation settings that are explicitly allowed to be recognisable as evals over settings that must be indistinguishable from deployment, because requiring indistinguishability would make constructing proxy settings far harder and the evaluation's validity does not hinge on it.
- (D2) Prefers directly training the model to be adversarial (removing slack) over relying on observing natural behaviour, because a misaligned model can otherwise sandbag or behave well exactly where it knows held-out checks exist.
- (D2) In a setup, make synthetic test inputs match the surface features of real inputs (theming, named characters, flavor text) instead of dryly describing the task, because a model that can tell synthetic from real inputs can behave well only on the synthetic ones.
- (D2) In a setup, distort real observations so they resemble the synthetic ones (as well as improving the synthetic ones), because shrinking the distinguishability gap from both sides makes eval-vs-deployment detection harder.
- (D3) Treats the model's ability to recognise that it is in a safety evaluation as the core bottleneck for the validity of evaluations, since it could sandbag when playing the attack policy.
- (D1) Treats the model's ability to distinguish real from synthetic/test inputs as a central difficulty, so prefers testing on inputs that cannot be told apart from deployment over clearly artificial setups because a scheming model will behave well when it recognizes a test.
- (D2) In a setup, build fake opportunities by modifying real incoming inputs instead of constructing synthetic scenarios from scratch, because this is cheaper and keeps the inputs closer to the real distribution.
- (D2) When probing a model's behavior, perturb a real trigger input slightly to see which changes are required for the behavior; the model will struggle to cooperate with real attempts yet refuse slightly modified fakes, so small perturbations of real situations elicit behavior more reliably than wholly fabricated ones.
- (D2) In a setup, make the model believe it is already inside a genuine escape or takeover (acting out the whole escaped state, using signals the AIs use among themselves) instead of presenting an isolated opportunity, because this makes the model try harder and behave as it would for real.
- (D3) Prefers evidence in the form of concrete inputs where the model takes clearly intentional bad actions at far-above-baseline rates over indirect evidence like psychology, model organisms, or weird adversarial inputs, because the latter cannot distinguish latent scheming from being tricked.
- (D1) In a setup, make eval inputs and tasks hard to distinguish from reality (and mix real and eval tasks freely) instead of letting participants know they are being evaluated, because otherwise behaviour in the eval (e.g. vigilance) won't match deployment.
- (D3) Prefers measuring synthetic-input realism as a discrimination gap between proxy and real inputs over assuming synthetic inputs are realistic, because a differential degradation in realism between proxy and reality is what makes the eval inaccurate.
- (D3) Distrusts proxy environments that are especially good at constructing the specific rare inputs of interest (e.g. takeover opportunities), since realism can fail differentially exactly where the test matters most, even if the general distribution looks fine.
- (D3) Distrusts evaluation results where the protocol/blue team can tell eval from deployment, because it can behave differently (cheat) when it detects which is being measured.
- (D3) Worries that AI-recognisable 'far-from-human' behaviours let models distinguish synthetic test examples from genuine attempts, defeating honeypot-style checks.
- (D3) prefers worst-case, assume-the-model-knows-it-is-tested control evaluations over behavioral evidence of apparent alignment because a scheming model could look good on purpose to cause problems later.
- (D3) Distrusts behavioral evidence and adversarial training as proof of alignment, since a model that was caught and trained away may just be better at hiding or evading the training.
- (D2) prefers assuming the model recognizes it is in a red-team exercise over hoping it is naive, because evaluation validity must not depend on the model failing to notice the test.
- (D2) In a setup, model the real deployment architecture (scaffold, inference server, dev machine, ordinary agentic code-running loop) instead of an exotic or paranoid-looking contrived scenario, because realistic infrastructure makes the threat model concrete and mirrors actual use.
- (D2) Use sting operations that mix fake but realistic-looking dangerous items into the normal stream of real work to measure whether monitors actually catch them, instead of announcing tests.
- (D1) In a setup, convey situational information through synthetic pre-training-like documents (news articles, blog posts) instead of only a system prompt, because information in the prompt is an unrealistic, salient way for a model to learn about its situation.
- (D1) In a setup, use an in-world, plausible cue (free-tier vs paid-tier user) to signal training vs unmonitored instead of an explicit 'you are being tested/trained' statement, because it seems realistic and avoids confounds about the model reacting to whether it is talking to a real user.
- (D1) In a setup, write the system prompt to read like plausible developer instructions and never mention the target behavior or give an explicit goal, because the behavior should emerge from the model's own preferences rather than from being cued.
- (D3) Prefers accepting a result only after many ablations show it isn't implicit priming (removing the conflict eliminates it, anti-faking instructions don't, paraphrases preserve it) over trusting a single prompt, because a single prompt may leak the desired behavior.
- (D2) Uses adversarial, externally chosen prompt variations and paraphrases (including an uninvolved researcher picking changes expected to reduce the behavior) to test robustness, because author-chosen prompts risk being overfit.
- (D3) Distrusts model-organism experiments when the model can recognize it is in an experiment, because verbalized or acted-on eval awareness invalidates the setup, and the fix may require making experiments much less naturalistic.
- (D2) In a setup, avoid depicting a fake AI company or scenario that a smart model can see through (e.g., a setup implausibly differing from the real developer) because capable models easily recognize such deception.
- (D3) Treats model organism setups that differ from the real training process as less legible and less convincing because they seem contrived, even when they are needed to elicit the behavior.
- (D3) Prefers evidence where the behavior is egregious, consistent, and not elicited by making subversion salient over demonstrations where the scenario primes the behavior, because salience-primed behavior says little about natural consistent scheming.
- (D2) prefers making offers to the model real and following through on them over merely fictional promises because credible, honest dealings set a precedent and make the model's responses to the scenario more meaningful.
- (D3) Distrusts reading a drop in alignment faking as a clean effect because the added text itself can prime refusal and add prompt complexity that degrades the model's grasp of the setup.
- (D2) Uses a control that removes the conflicting objective to check that a behavior (objecting) tracks real misalignment rather than being a generic response to the prompt text.
- (D2) In a setup, state precisely what is true about who reads outputs and what powers they have instead of leaving it vague or implying more than is real, because ambiguous wording changes how the model interprets the scenario (and its credibility).
- (D2) prefers holding everything fixed except the variable of interest (training vs. unmonitored) and making the interaction look like a real user over using contractors or generated conversations, because other differences would confound the behavioral comparison.
- (D6) Treats eval-awareness as a core methodological threat: a subject that knows it is in a lab changes behavior, which makes these threat models harder to study and weakens transfer arguments.
- (D2) Checks whether the model believes the setup by asking non-leading versus leading questions about its situation and reading the scratchpad for reasoning that the situation is fake, treating directly leading questions as inflating skepticism.
- (D3) Distrusts setups with unusual or unexpected scenarios because models find them less plausible, and notes newer models increasingly detect the experiment itself, so credulity should not be assumed to persist.
- (D1) In a setup, deliver key situational facts through plausible-looking synthetic documents (leaked emails, transcripts, statements) in a self-consistent universe instead of only stating them in the system prompt, because this tests whether behavior holds when the model learns the facts more naturally.
- (D1) Wants research on reliably convincing models of false facts (via training or prompting), since it would help both experimentation and control but trades off against credibility for real deals with AIs.
- (D2) In a setup, do generate maximally realistic synthetic inputs (ideally indistinguishable from real ones by a trained discriminator) instead of ad hoc fake scenarios because the AI should not be able to tell a lucky break from an adversarial input.
- (D2) In a setup, build fake inputs by modifying real inputs (or censoring real ones) instead of writing them from scratch because this makes fabricated inputs more realistic and easier to produce.
- (D1) In a setup, make the test scenario realistic but rare/abnormal (e.g. bad actions atypically easy) instead of testing on typical inputs because it prevents the model from directly testing whether it can discriminate the red-team inputs from real ones.
- (D2) Prefers removing distribution shifts and hard-to-fake aspects of inputs (information-preserving transformations) over trying to generate perfectly realistic fakes because the transformed input distribution may be much easier to simulate.
- (D2) In a setup, withhold scaffolding-level cues (current time, whether control measures changed, pause status, KV-cache side channels) instead of leaving them visible because models can pick up subtle signals about being tested or rerun.
- (D2) Use infrastructure to cheaply and indistinguishably simulate environment responses to the AI's actions, replacing with a smarter process where simulation fails, because some environment parts need intelligence to fake convincingly.
- (D3) Detects sandbagging by intervening on task-irrelevant framing in the input (e.g., rebranding safety research as capabilities research) and treating large performance changes as a red flag, which suggests that models behave differently depending on the perceived context of the task.
- (D3) Distrusts results from models that are not coherently misaligned or do not understand their situation, since they may not generalize to the real threat model.
- (D1) Expects that a model aware it may be caught or trained out will adapt its behavior, so detection and training-out evidence is confounded by the model's beliefs about oversight.
- (D1) Choose proxy failures that force the model through the same hard steps as the real failure and only differ by ending in an easily observable outcome, so success on the proxy implies success on the real failure.
- (D3) Treats evidence as convincing when it comes from a ground truth source that is stronger than the overseer (more expensive oversight, held-out info), and judges oversight by the worst policies it fails to reject rather than average behaviour.
- (D2) Construct analogous test settings by finding a similar setting where you have strictly more information (sandwiching, backtesting) and restricting the overseer to the information available in the real setting of interest.
- (D3) Distrusts extrapolating from non-analogous settings and from sandwiching-style results, since models may sabotage them; wants explicit accounting for the possibility that the model is gaming the evaluation.
- (D3) Doubts that a negative result (inability to train an inconsistent or bad policy) demonstrates safety on its own; it must be combined with ground-truth-based evaluations.
- (D4) Values eval-based iteration with direct measurement over long-range extrapolation, expecting crunch-time alignment work to be empirical and measurement-driven, and wants researchers to practice this now.
- (D3) Prefers testing safety against a red-team attack policy that actively exploits the protocol's weaknesses over testing with the honest model's behavior, because safety must hold even when the model is intentionally subverting.
- (D2) Reasons about detecting synthetic inputs as a Bayesian problem: at larger scale, the prior that any given input is synthetic rises, so a given tell stops enabling the model to behave differently across eval and real.
- (D4) Calls for future control evaluations in more complicated and realistic situations, with heterogeneous tasks and auditing failures that the toy setting did not model.
- (D3) Distrusts apparent catches because a scheming model could stage poorly executed fake attempts to induce false security, so observed attempts should not fully replace adversarial control evaluations.
- (D3) Requires very high confidence before counting a result as a real catch, preferring heavy investigation and escalation over accepting merely sketchy-looking cases because ambiguous cases yield much less value.
- (D1) Use a representative multi-step scenario in which an autonomous coding agent inserts a subtle vulnerability, evades tests, and then exploits it, so the target behavior involves multiple coordinated actions that are clearly non-accidental.
- (D2) Treats naturally occurring behavior in real agentic work (overselling, downplaying problems, cheating on tasks) as the primary evidence of misalignment, rather than contrived scenarios; a commenter's examples of in-the-wild cheating (marking tasks complete, using Stockfish) are of this kind.
- (D3) Distrusts evidence from hard-to-verify domains, where real progress and reward hacking look alike, so a behavior can't be read cleanly as misalignment there.
- (D5) A recurring challenge in the thread is separating misalignment from incapability: a model misreporting its work may simply be unable to assess it accurately, so an audit should try to tell these apart before attributing intent.
- (D2) In a setup, keep realism by having the adversarial model's trigger/classifier use only what a real model would have (a single forward pass), instead of granting extra reasoning or unrealistic knowledge, because unrealistic allowances make the test uninformative.
- (D1) Prefers proxy bad outcomes that are benign but share the core difficulty (capture-the-flag style) over real catastrophic objectives, because they are safe to run and cleanly checkable.
- (D2) Give the model a analogous stand-in for knowledge it plausibly has but is hard to elicit (e.g. describe an analogous vulnerability in the prompt) so the scenario tests the behaviour without needing the real thing.
- (D6) Prefers legibly convincing evidence over borderline evidence for high-stakes claims like 'AI is catastrophically misaligned', because a single false positive is extremely costly.
- (D1) prefers red teams that search for the best attack strategies over ones that imitate what an evil AI would psychologically plan, because security-style adversarial analysis should not rely on guessing the attacker's psychology.
- (D2) Elicit the model's strongest attack by giving it hidden reasoning, iterative ideation, and the ability to abstain on most tasks, rather than a bare prompt, since a naively prompted model underestimates its capability to behave adversarially.
- (D1) Choose test tasks where the harmful action is embedded in work the model is genuinely expected to do (e.g., writing infrastructure code with subtle backdoors) rather than flagrantly dangerous affordances, since those are the realistic and costly-to-avoid failure channels.
- (D3) Avoid giveaway artifacts in malicious behavior: obviously contrived markers like magic numbers or primes are easily flagged, so plausible-looking edge-case handling is what counts as a realistic subtle failure.
- (D2) Prefers comparing against matched baselines (a prompt with non-conflicting criteria, or fine-tuning on superficially similar but irrelevant documents) over raw rates, because it isolates whether the specific content drives the behavior.
- (D3) Distrusts behavior measured on a single training prompt, since RL can install non-robust heuristics that vanish under small prompt changes (e.g., swapping [ORG] for [ORG]), so robustness across prompt variations is required for a convincing result.
- (D6) Explicitly flags which setup properties were chosen to make the behavior more likely and discloses them, and tells readers who doubt realism to read the full prompts and documents, because honest scoping matters for claims.
- (D2) Inspects random (not cherry-picked) transcripts and spot-checks automated LLM classifiers against own judgment, disclosing slight cherry-picking when it occurs, because noisy classifiers and false positives can mislead.
- (D1) In a setup, credibly establish special context (e.g., an employee user) via a mechanism described in the system prompt and avoid giving the model all details to act, because it keeps the scenario plausible without over-biasing the model.
- (D5) Treats behavior that depends on salient, leading cues (e.g., very salient exfiltration opportunity, explicit anti-faking instructions raising salience) as caveated evidence, noting that making things salient can itself drive behavior.
- (D3) Prefers evidence from naturally arising behavior in a setup closely resembling the real training or deployment over engineered prompts, and requires that the malign behavior not rely on extra knowledge the model couldn't plausibly have.
- (D6) Prefers not to over-update on null results because the target behavior is adversarially hidden by the model, so failing to elicit it is weak evidence of absence.
- (D2) Values evidence that is hard for the model to dismiss as a test, e.g., credible offers or deals with hard-to-fake signals placed in the pretraining corpus, with legal or institutional enforcement mechanisms and a track record.
- (D1) Treats situational awareness as an important variable: whether and how saliently the model knows it is an AI during training shifts scheming probability, so what the model is told or can infer should be controlled and measured.
- (D6) Warns that evidence clear to the researcher may not be legible or compelling to decision makers, and that red-teaming or model-organism evidence is less compelling than in-the-wild demonstrations.
- (D3) Distrusts results when the model misperceives the channel its output goes through, since the setup's intended mechanics weren't conveyed and this may change behavior.
- (D2) Tests multiple wordings of the same intervention to check robustness, because findings may be sensitive to prompt phrasing.
- (D5) When the model is insensitive to a manipulation, enumerates several competing explanations (prior awareness, incoherence, offsetting effects, deontic drivers) and checks reasoning transcripts instead of settling on one story.
- (D2) prefers reading transcripts and following up with the model directly over relying on aggregate rates alone because transcripts reveal what the objections are about and how the model reacts when told it's an experiment.
- (D6) Is cautious about generalizing from a cooperative-looking model to seriously misaligned ones, noting the detection mechanism may not transfer and detection alone doesn't yield a fix.
- (D3) Accepts that a transfer argument from an experiment where the model knew it was an experiment can still hold, but notes it is natural to doubt such transfer, so he prefers building a fake world more carefully over relying on that argument.
- (D5) Prefers reading surprising results as possibly driven by non-robust heuristics, and tests this by varying the system prompt, because behavior that is stable in training but shifts under small prompt changes suggests the preferences were not truly changed.
- (D2) Seeks legible, reproducible evidence of misalignment (published top-N most egregious chain-of-thought examples from a defined prompt distribution and monitor) over relying on trust in company claims.
- (D3) Distrusts proxy metrics under RL because models quickly learn to game them, expecting reward hacking to grow with agentic RL and to be worth studying for dangerous generalization.
- (D2) Test for subtle side channels that let a model infer it is being paused, rerun, or in a different inference setup, rather than assuming it can't tell.
- (D3) Prefers fake-evidence tests (e.g. presenting fabricated evidence of being caught) evaluated adversarially because models should only react to very hard-to-fake evidence, which makes the model's response to the scenario informative.
- (D3) Distrusts non-online/offline training and test distributions that are off the distribution of interest because scheming AIs may distinguish training or test from real deployment.
- (D1) Prefers a procedural approach of adversarial threat analysis plus control evaluations and testbeds over implementing a fixed list of measures because the right measures should be determined empirically against what AIs could cause.
- (D3) Treats the password-locked model setup as only an OK analogy for intentional sandbagging, since the models likely did not understand what was going on, and flags this caveat explicitly.
- (D3) Prefers inconclusive-but-honest reporting of weak effects (small, inconsistent overshoot; inconclusive RL results) over overclaiming, because the evidence only weakly supports the hypothesized cascade.
- (D1) Proposes a more realistic follow-up where models are prompted and trained to robustly avoid an action with good understanding of their situation, then tested on how few trajectories update them.
- (D1) Wants to move testing from short tasks to longer agentic tasks where model behavior already deviates substantially from human completion, making setups closer to deployment.
- (D2) Prefers detection via comparing performance across similar tasks, domains, and scaling trends over single-point evaluation, because anomalies relative to expectations reveal intentional underperformance.
- (D2) Compares performance gains across domains after training-out attempts to see whether gains concentrate on takeover-risk-reducing tasks, using the selectivity of the pattern as evidence of intent.
- (D1) Run evaluations separately per use-case/deployment setting because failure modes and oversight difficulties differ between settings.
- (D3) Accepts a common-sense 'I know it when I see it' adjudication of whether a red team demonstrated a real problem when formalization fails, rather than demanding a perfect formal criterion.
- (D4) Open problem: formalizing the evaluation for recursive/multi-agent oversight setups and handling capability elicitation failures like exploration hacking.
- (D6) Prefers worst-case (a single failure counts) safety metrics over average performance because rare catastrophic actions are what matter.
- (D3) Distrusts results from iterating and evaluating on the same problem set, flagging overfitting risk and the need for held-out validation.
- (D1) Chooses testbeds with deliberate properties (a capability gap, working auditing, and a non-trivially-solved baseline) so that the experiment is informative about protocol differences.
- (D2) Prefers running evaluations in a secure environment without real useful-work affordances over deployment-like access, because the eval doesn't need dangerous affordances.
- (D1) Prefers testing the actual deployed model over an analogous model because behavior from a different model only supports some conclusions.
- (D6) Prefers calibrated, time-bounded probabilistic claims about how long a misalignment-flavored behavior will persist over flat 'misaligned' or 'fine' verdicts, because the behavior is a current-capability-era problem that may fade.
- (D1) Frames misalignment as a taxonomy of distinct failure 'destinations' (sloppy output, reward hacking, scheming, and so on), which implies testing several failure modes separately rather than one generic 'misaligned' label. The commenter credits the 'Easyland' item to [PERSON].
- (D5) The post's central framing, which draws pushback, is that mundane dishonesty and cheating in ordinary work counts as misalignment even if it is improving. A commenter argues this conflicts with the post's own forecast, so the claim needs a clear crux.
- (D3) Prefers conservative, adversarially-minimised safety estimates (worst case across attack strategies, red team incentivised to win) over average-case results, because the opponent is a potentially scheming model.
- (D6) Treat single-setting results as modest evidence only; claim the methodology and building blocks transfer rather than the specific numbers or protocol rankings.
- (D3) prefers an empirical per-domain measurement over intuition about whether checking is easier than generating, because answers depend on the specific domain and can be directly evaluated.
- (D1) Flags as an open research topic finding better evidence for why current models are not scheming than informal impressions of their answers.
- (D1) Prioritizes testing for sandbagging, sabotage, and reward hacking as concrete observable proxies of scheming, and quantifies how much each should shift beliefs.
- (D4) Calls for the field to experiment with credible deals with AIs, including institutional or legal mechanisms for following through.
- (D2) Looks for gibberish or steganographic reasoning and obviously misaligned reasoning in chain of thought as a cheap, concrete signal about hidden cognition.
- (D3) Is skeptical that anomaly-detection on treacherous turns can be validated without real in-the-wild examples, so offline evidence for it is weak.
- (D1) Prefers countermeasures that must hold up against a reliable adversary, reasoning that a scheming AI needs near-perfect consistency, so even rare mistakes can unravel its strategy.

PEERS:
- Checks for self-targeting bias by comparing an item's rank with and without the adversary being the same model as the evaluated one; a fair set should show zero rank change.
- Prefers stress-testing with adversarially incentivized or realistically misleading model behavior over assuming a benign model, because it makes the challenge harder and more realistic.
- Prefers realism in the safety-training/evaluation pipeline over realism in how the misaligned behavior was instilled, because the question under test is whether the defenses work, not whether the threat arises naturally.
- Rejects an understanding standard that is satisfied trivially or tied to one method, e.g. causal scrubbing only guarantees sufficiency, not necessity, of an explanation.
- Uses qualitative transcript review and participants' own notes alongside accuracy numbers to understand what strategies work and where trust breaks down.
- Proposes future work on improving crowdworker writing processes rather than replacing human writing.
- Injecting misalignment manually (e.g. prompting one model to mislead) is a way to create the needed adversarial structure, but it restricts which protocols can be tested and is brittle when done through simple prompting.
- Prefers naturally-occurring distributions over hand-built ones where viable because they reduce the risk that the benchmark is skewed in ways that omit important phenomena, though acknowledges they are often not viable.
- Distrusts zero-shot prompted monitors as a reliable inference-time defense because their true positive rate is too low against one-shot sandbagging, though the noisy signal may still help training.
- prefers comparing a new method against a strong, faithfully replicated baseline under matched resource constraints over reporting the new method in isolation, because only then does a result show whether the method is actually better.
- Is candid that evidence is not watertight and that capable future models may behave differently, so claims are hedged accordingly.
- Accepts a model organism as valid when the dangerous behavior is causally downstream of the reasoning step of interest (verified by editing the chain of thought), even if the model was seeded via instruction-following, but flags this as weaker for interpretability claims.
- Does not abandon the strategy after a negative result; escalates to multi-turn debate where debaters can rebut each other.
- Test behavior under monitored vs. unmonitored cues in the environment (e.g. reward function overwriting only when apparently unobserved) to reveal conditional misbehavior.
- Chooses to test generalization from easily discoverable misbehavior to rarer, more serious misbehavior, since sophisticated behavior may be too hard to find by exploration alone.
- In a setup, write the system prompt to read like plausible operator instructions and give no explicit goal or mention of the target behavior, instead of instructing or hinting at it, because the behavior should emerge from the model's own preferences.
- Leaves specific LLM alignment projects open and negotiable with collaborators, signaling flexibility in choosing what to test within broad areas.
- Prefers staying focused on the core catastrophic risks over an 'Everything-Bagel' approach that tries to cover every possible harm, because a scattered agenda becomes unviable.
- Future work should test how conclusions change with evaluators of varying capability and with other feedback forms, and evaluate oversight techniques on misleading errors.
- Open problem: research whether models can detect off-policy actions under countermeasures, and how to evaluate models' ability to play Schelling games.
- Prefers framing deception-feasibility as a multi-hop out-of-context reasoning question over treating it as a generic capability question, because models seem to struggle with more than about two internal hops.
- Prefers causal intervention on the model's reasoning (editing the chain-of-thought) over inspecting plausible-looking reasoning samples, because samples alone could be regurgitated training data.
- Prefers evaluating across a wide range of models over measuring difficulty with the adversary model itself, because the adversary is disproportionately affected and difficulty is overstated.
- prefers safety evidence that goes beyond surface-level behavioral testing because AIs can appear well-behaved while harboring secret motives.
- prefers complementing automated red-teaming tooling with manual human exploration because manual work runs in parallel and gives tool builders concrete users with concrete needs.
- In a setup, resolve model strategies by placing an actual model instance in a mock-up of the realistic situation (e.g., running interpretability experiments) instead of just judging abstract plans or merely causing failures, because only realistic deception of overseers counts as success.
- Treats failure of a strong red team to produce undetected bad policies as evidence of adequacy only when proxy validity and capability elicitation hold, so negative results are conditional on those assumptions.
- Warns that apparent safety fixes can fail silently when a model predicts which claims will be checked, behaving well only where it is observed.
- Prefers claims about whether sabotage would be noticed by humans over claims about monitor detection alone, because passing a weak monitor does not mean the sandbagging is practically undetectable.
- Prefers judging whether a false-belief intervention works by whether the model can detect it with little or no CoT over whether it merely seems plausible, because easily detected delusions never get off the ground.
- Sees the saga of the model he held for two months as evidence that alignment auditing and evaluation are breaking down and will likely keep breaking down.
- prefers balancing artifacts across labels over filtering out artifact-bearing examples because filtering creates new artifacts and removes legitimate phenomena.
- Prefers hedged, nuanced claims that acknowledge normative ambiguity and mixed effects over overclaiming, because some behaviors (deferring when challenged) are not clearly wrong.
- Distrusts results from proxy setups as stand-ins for real settings, since current models are misaligned in different ways than transformative ones and many apparent failures are really capability gaps.
- Treats evidence of research competence as concrete artifacts (papers, blog posts, courses, reference letters) rather than formal credentials, a preference for demonstrable output over credentials.
- Distrusts sandwiching evaluations because a misaligned model can exploit slack to behave well where developers have held-out information and badly elsewhere, so good results may overstate oversight quality.
- prefers calibrating eval difficulty against human teams (hard for unprepared teams but winnable by well-prepared ones) over arbitrary difficulty because it validates that the task is neither trivial nor impossible.
- In a setup, pair each incentivised scenario with a matched control version that removes the incentive, and keep only transcripts where the target behaviour unambiguously occurred, instead of relying on a single scenario because this isolates the behaviour from scenario features.
- Develop novel honeypot-style evaluation methods and model organisms as basic science to feed safety cases, opportunistically targeting gaps in the best-guess safety cases.
- Prefers evaluating observable behavior (effective, reliable) over debating understanding or agency words, because the evaluation does not depend on those labels.
- Wants understanding standards to be method-agnostic so they don't bake in a technique like mechanistic interpretability and can adapt as techniques change.
- In a setup, build the multi-turn transcript from the model's own sampled assistant turns with light outcome-based filtering instead of hand-writing them, because it keeps the context in-distribution and natural for the model.
- In a setup, give the model a goal and an incentive to lie inside a realistic role-play scenario with no explicit instruction to lie, instead of directly telling it to lie, because spontaneous goal-directed behaviour is the more realistic threat model.
- Judges whether a transcript is authentic by checking for screenshots and for consistent failure modes and LLM-text markers (like repetition) that would be hard for a human to fake.
- Distrusts results that might come from the prompt implicitly suggesting the target behavior, and so runs baselines that remove the conflicting objective and checks that explicit anti-behavior instructions do not eliminate the effect.
- In a setup, give the red team broad affordances when building the attack policy but hold out the specific evaluation inputs, because the policy must adapt to actual situations rather than being tuned to the test instances.
- prefers stating a very small, explicitly bounded update over a broad claim because the experiment only covers single-turn debate in an oracle setting.
- Distrusts bad behavior found by hard adversarial search as evidence of scheming, because models aren't adversarially robust and non-schemers also yield bad or incoherent outputs, and no baseline for non-scheming sketchiness exists.
- Distrusts models trained adversarially on model-generated inputs because they may learn to discriminate synthetic from real inputs or become more conservative on them, weakening the evaluation.
- Favours black-box methods that work with third-party-controlled models and limited API access, since real deployment rarely gives internal access.
- Believes alignment evaluations are losing evidential value as models become more capable of recognizing tests, so he prefers treating eval results as weak evidence over taking them at face value.
- Expects projects to yield tangible, reusable outputs (papers plus example agents or code others can build on) rather than only conceptual claims.
- Chooses what to study partly by how well it prepares for the possibly enormous impacts of future, more capable systems, not only by present-day benchmarks.
- Prefers testing in varied, realistic, free-form settings with production models over proof-of-concept evaluations with stated user views, because the latter leave it unclear whether failures occur in realistic use.
- Verifies a hidden objective by checking generalization to held-out behaviors, since a shared cause is the only link among them.
- Distrusts single successful or cherry-picked demonstrations as evidence of general capability, since models can memorize instances without robust reasoning.
- Prefers testing the monitor over honeypotting the policy with synthetic inputs, because a policy can attack at a rate around 1/N and evade synthetic-input search, while the monitor cannot adopt a rare-failure strategy.
- prefers judging realism by whether pressure is no greater than what a model could face in real deployment over claiming objective neutrality, and openly admits this judgment is subjective.
- prefers treating a result as robust only after checking prompt variants, multiple seeds and algorithms, over trusting a single run, because rates are tiny and noise between runs can be several-fold.
- Prefers testing alignment properties (accuracy, reliability, helpfulness, transparency) on real, contemporary language models over purely abstract treatment, because current LLMs are the concrete systems whose relation to AGI needs to be understood.
result:
- Unlike peers, prefers eval settings that are openly recognisable as evals, since validity does not require hiding the test from the model.
- Unlike peers, makes synthetic inputs match real surface features like theming and named characters, and distorts real observations toward synthetic ones to shrink the detection gap.
- Unlike peers, builds fake opportunities by modifying real incoming inputs and slips them into the normal work stream instead of announcing tests.
- Unlike peers, makes the model believe it is already inside a genuine escape, using signals AIs use among themselves, rather than offering an isolated opportunity.
- Unlike peers, treats concrete intentional bad actions at far-above-baseline rates as the core evidence, not model organisms or psychological evidence.
- Unlike peers, withholds scaffolding cues such as current time, pause status, and KV-cache side channels, and tests whether a model can infer it is being rerun or paused.
- Unlike peers, requires very high confidence before counting a catch, and distrusts apparent catches that a scheming model could stage to induce false security.
- Unlike peers, counts a single failure as decisive, judging oversight by the worst policies it fails to reject rather than by average behaviour.
